Bitcoin/Gold Ratio

This ratio shows how many ounces of gold are equivalent to one Bitcoin. It divides the Bitcoin daily close by the gold daily close on the same calendar date.

Why investors watch this ratio

A rising Bitcoin/Gold ratio means Bitcoin is strengthening relative to gold. A falling ratio means gold is gaining relative strength against Bitcoin.

The comparison can add context to changing risk appetite, but it does not establish the cause of either asset's move and is not a standalone trading signal.

Bitcoin versus gold: two different store-of-value theses

Bitcoin and gold are often grouped together as stores of value or inflation hedges, but they behave quite differently in practice. Gold has a 5,000-year track record as a monetary metal, minimal correlation with risk assets over long periods, and a stable annual supply growth of roughly 1–2% from mining. Bitcoin has a 15-year track record, high correlation with risk assets during market stress, and a fixed maximum supply of 21 million coins with predictable halvings every four years that cut new issuance. In crisis periods — the March 2020 COVID crash, the 2022 rate-rise drawdown — Bitcoin has typically sold off alongside equities before recovering, while gold has held its value better in the initial shock. Over multi-year bull markets for digital assets, Bitcoin's higher volatility and growth-asset characteristics have tended to push the ratio sharply higher.

Historical ratio moves and what drove them

The Bitcoin/Gold ratio has gone through wide swings since Bitcoin first traded at scale in 2013. At Bitcoin's 2017 peak near $20,000 with gold around $1,300, the ratio reached roughly 15 ounces of gold per Bitcoin. It then fell sharply through 2018 as Bitcoin sold off 80% while gold held. At Bitcoin's 2021 peak near $69,000 with gold around $1,800, the ratio briefly exceeded 38. In the 2022 bear market, it compressed back to around 8–10 as Bitcoin fell more than 70% while gold held near $1,800. In 2026, with gold trading near all-time highs above $3,000 per ounce and Bitcoin in a new cycle, the ratio reflects whichever asset is leading the current macro narrative.

Risk-on versus risk-off: reading the ratio in context

The Bitcoin/Gold ratio can serve as a rough barometer of market risk appetite. When investors are willing to hold volatile digital assets and allocate to growth, Bitcoin tends to outperform gold and the ratio rises. When the macro environment shifts toward risk aversion — central banks tightening, financial stress emerging, geopolitical uncertainty rising — gold tends to outperform Bitcoin and the ratio falls. This is not a mechanical rule, and there are periods where both assets move in the same direction. But the ratio's direction is often more informative than either asset's absolute price level in isolation.

Some investors use a rising Bitcoin/Gold ratio as a signal that speculative capital is flowing back into risk assets more broadly, treating it as a leading indicator for broader equity strength. Others use extreme compression of the ratio as a signal that the market has become defensively positioned and may be positioned for a recovery in risk assets. Neither interpretation is reliable enough to use as a standalone trading signal, but the ratio adds one more data point to a broader macro picture.
